---
title: Area-Level SAE Modeling (Fay--Herriot)
subtitle: "A Bayesian spatio-temporal extension"
---

::: {.callout-note title="Theory in brief"}
The Fay--Herriot model treats each direct estimate as a noisy observation of the true area-time quantity:

$$
\hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt} = \mu_{jt} + e_{jt}, \qquad
e_{jt} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \psi_{jt}),
$$

where $\psi_{jt}$ is the sampling variance estimated from the survey design. The latent area-time mean is then modelled using predictors and an area random effect:

$$
\mu_{jt} = \alpha + \mathbf{x}_{jt}^{T}\boldsymbol{\beta} + u_j + v_t.
$$

Here $u_j$ borrows strength across areas while the target remains the area-time quantity $\mu_{jt}$. The area effect can be replaced by a structured spatial effect, and a temporal effect $v_t$ can be added to represent wave-to-wave dependence. 
The fitted model gives an area-time estimate by combining the direct estimate with the model prediction:

$$
\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{FH}}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\mu_{jt} \mid \hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt}, x_{jt}).
$$
:::

```{r}
#| label: fh-setup
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(spdep)
library(INLA)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(scales)

base_path <- here::here("data")
domain_frame <- read_csv(file.path(base_path, "clean", "domain_msoayear.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
share_label <- label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)
pp_label <- label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale = 100, suffix = " pp")

msoa_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  rename(area_id = all_of("MSOA21CD")) |>
  filter(str_starts(area_id, "W")) |>
  arrange(area_id)

```

```{r}
#| label: fh-plot-config
#| echo: false
variance_label <- label_number(accuracy = 0.0001)
missing_fill <- "grey85"
diverging_low <- "#2166ac"
diverging_high <- "#b2182b"

map_text_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
  axis.title.y = element_text(
    size = 12,
    face = "bold",
    angle = 90,
    margin = margin(r = 15)
  ),
  legend.title = element_text(size = 10),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 9)
)

chart_text_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
  strip.text = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
  axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
  axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 12)
)

map_annotation_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5, colour = "grey30")
)
```

## Estimation approach {.unnumbered}

{{< include assets/target-estimand.qmd >}}

Area-level SAE starts from the direct estimates created in the previous step. The Fay--Herriot model treats each direct estimate for an area-time cell, an *MSOA-year cell* in this example, as a noisy observation of the underlying frequent-cycling rate, using its sampling variance to control how much confidence the model places in that value.

The model then borrows strength across MSOAs and survey years using spatial and temporal random effects. We then test whether mean adult age, car-access household share, and population density improve fit beyond the temporal-spatial structure.

## Prepare modelling data

First we import the complete area-time direct-estimates, then load the area predictors.

```{r}
#| label: fh-load-direct
direct_bike <- read_csv(file.path(base_path, "freqbike_estimates_direct.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(
    all_of(c(
      "area_id",
      "msoa_name",
      "time_id",
      "direct_estimate",
      "variance",
      "n"
    ))
  )

head(direct_bike)
```
```{r}
#| label: fh-load-predictors
area_predictors <- read_csv(file.path(base_path, "clean", "areapred_freqbike.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(
    all_of(c(
      "area_id",
      "scaled_mean_age_adult",
      "scaled_car_access_hhshare",
      "scaled_population_density"
    ))
  )
head(area_predictors)
```

The missing or zero sampling variances of direct estimates need to be handled, because it controls how much weight each direct estimate receives in the FH model.

- For area-time cells without a direct estimate or variance, we assign the maximum observed positive sampling variance, signalling high uncertainty. Their estimates will be mostly determined by the model predictions.
- Because the outcome is binary (`1` for cycling frequently, `0` otherwise), very small samples can produce a variance of `0` when all sampled respondents give the same response. We also assign these cells the maximum observed positive sampling variance.

```{r}
#| label: fh-variance
#| code-fold: false

max_variance <- max(direct_bike$variance[direct_bike$variance > 0], na.rm = TRUE)

direct_bike_model <- direct_bike |>
  mutate(
    adj_variance = case_when(
      is.na(direct_estimate) ~ max_variance,
      is.na(variance) ~ max_variance,
      variance <= 1e-8 ~ max_variance,
      TRUE ~ variance
    )
  )
```

`INLA` uses numeric indices to encode space and time, so we create `time_inla_id` and `area_inla_id` to index survey years and MSOAs. We also provide an adjacency graph for the structured spatial effect. Here, we use Queen contiguity, where two MSOAs are treated as neighbours if their boundaries touch at either an edge or a point.

```{r}
#| label: fh-index
#| code-fold: false

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)
```
```{r}
#| label: fh-graph
#| code-fold: false

msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)
```

![](assets/spatial_weights_example.png)

Finally, we assemble the modelling data for `INLA` by combining the direct estimates with the area predictors and the numeric indices for the temporal and spatial effects.

```{r}
#| label: fh-model-data

model_data <- direct_bike_model |>
  left_join(area_predictors, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  arrange(time_id, area_inla_id)

head(model_data)
```

## Fit and evaluate models

Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct estimation is passed to `INLA` as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight. We define these model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates using `INLA`.

| Model | Name | Specifications |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | +TempSpatial | Temporal and spatial effect |
| M2 | +AvgAge | M1 plus mean adult age |
| M3 | +PopDensCarAccess | M2 plus population density and share of HH with car access |

The choice of spatial and temporal models should reflect assumptions about how residual variation is structured across space and time.

| Temporal model | Description |
|---|---|
| `rw1` | First-order random walk: smooths neighbouring time periods. |
| `rw2` | Second-order random walk: smooths changes in the trend over longer time series. |
| `ar1` | Autoregressive effect: assumes correlation decays with time distance, so closer years are more similar than distant years. |

| Spatial model | Description |
|---|---|
| `besag` | Smooths estimates across neighbouring areas, capturing spatially structured residual variation. |
| `bym2` | Updated BYM model with a mixing parameter, `phi`, which indicates how much residual variation is spatially structured. |

With only three survey years, `rw1` is suitable because it smooths neighbouring waves. Spatially, `bym2` is appropriate because it allows the model to borrow strength from neighbouring MSOAs while still capturing unstructured local variability.

```{r}
#| label: fh-fit
#| code-fold: false

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m2_formula <- update(m1_formula, . ~ . +
  scaled_mean_age_adult
)

m3_formula <- update(m2_formula, . ~ . +
  scaled_population_density +
  scaled_car_access_hhshare
)


model_formulas <- list(
  "M1 +TempSpatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +AvgAge" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +PopDensCarAccess" = m3_formula
)

fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$adj_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)
```

:::{.callout-note}
When fitting area-level FH models with `INLA`, these arguments are needed:

- `control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE)` returns fitted values for every row. In an area-level model, these are the final estimates for each area-time row.
- `scale` passes the inverse sampling variance to `INLA`, so less precise direct estimates get smoothed more.
- `control.family` fixes the Gaussian residual precision because the direct-estimate variances already provide the uncertainty.
- `control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)` requests WAIC for comparing model fit and stores the configuration needed for posterior sampling.
:::

To compare the fitted models' overall performance, we use `WAIC` or (Widely Applicable Information Criterion) as a first check. It is a global predictive-fit measure returned by `INLA`; lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity.

```{r}
#| label: fh-waic
model_waic <- imap_dfr(
  fh_fits,
  \(fit, model_name) {
    tibble(
      model = model_name,
      waic = fit$waic$waic,
      eff_params = fit$waic$p.eff
    )
  }
)|>
  arrange(waic)
model_waic
```

Based on this comparison, M2, which includes average MSOA age, performs best. This suggests that differences in the age profile of MSOAs explain much of the variation in the direct estimates, and that adding car access or population density provides little additional improvement in model fit.

## Estimation with posterior draws

The selected `INLA` fit gives an approximation to the joint posterior distribution. We draw from that posterior so each draw gives one plausible fitted value for every MSOA-year cell. Summarising these draws gives the posterior mean, variance, and credible interval used in the maps and exported estimates.

```{r}
#| label: fh-results
#| code-fold: false

# Best model selection
fh_best_model <- model_waic |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(model)
fh_selected_fit <- fh_fits[[fh_best_model]]

# 300 draws from the model's posteriors.
set.seed(100)
fh_posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(
  n = 300,
  result = fh_selected_fit
)

# Extract the fitted FH estimate for each MSOA-year cell from every posterior draw
predictor_rows <- startsWith(
  rownames(fh_posterior_draws[[1]]$latent),
  "Predictor"
)
fh_draw_matrix <- sapply(fh_posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  as.numeric(draw$latent[predictor_rows, 1])
})

# Summarise the draws into the exported estimate, variance, and 95% credible interval 
model_output_frame <- model_data |>
  select(area_id, time_id, msoa_name, direct_estimate, variance, n)

final_fh_results <- model_output_frame |>
  bind_cols(
    tibble(
      fh_estimate = rowMeans(fh_draw_matrix),
      fh_variance = apply(fh_draw_matrix, 1, var),
      fh_lower = apply(fh_draw_matrix, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025),
      fh_upper = apply(fh_draw_matrix, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975)
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    fh_ci_width = fh_upper - fh_lower
  )

head(final_fh_results)
```

```{r}
#| label: fh-map
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 16
#| out-width: "100%"

final_fh_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(final_fh_results, by = "area_id")
fh_estimate_limits <- range(final_fh_results$fh_estimate, na.rm = TRUE)
fh_ci_width_limits <- c(0, max(final_fh_results$fh_ci_width, na.rm = TRUE))
fh_wave_years <- sort(unique(final_fh_results$time_id))

plot_fh_estimate <- function(wave) {
  final_fh_map_data |>
    filter(time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = fh_estimate), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(
      option = "magma",
      limits = fh_estimate_limits,
      labels = share_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Share"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

plot_fh_ci_width <- function(wave) {
  final_fh_map_data |>
    filter(time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = fh_ci_width), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_distiller(
      palette = "Oranges",
      direction = 1,
      limits = fh_ci_width_limits,
      labels = pp_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "95% CI width"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

fh_estimate_maps <- lapply(fh_wave_years, plot_fh_estimate)
fh_uncertainty_maps <- lapply(fh_wave_years, plot_fh_ci_width)

fh_estimate_maps[[1]] <- fh_estimate_maps[[1]] + ylab("Final estimate")
fh_uncertainty_maps[[1]] <- fh_uncertainty_maps[[1]] + ylab("95% CI width")

for (i in seq_len(length(fh_wave_years) - 1)) {
  fh_estimate_maps[[i]] <- fh_estimate_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
  fh_uncertainty_maps[[i]] <- fh_uncertainty_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

wrap_plots(c(fh_estimate_maps, fh_uncertainty_maps), ncol = length(fh_wave_years)) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Share of adults who cycle for transport frequently",
    subtitle = paste0("Selected FH model (", fh_best_model, ") and 95% CI width"),
    theme = map_annotation_theme
  )
```

Here we see that the Fay--Herriot estimates produce a less jagged pattern across neighbouring areas and clearer broad regional structure than the direct estimates. At the same time, weaker survey coverage can still leave year-specific patterns in the modelled estimates. The generally higher 2023 estimates are consistent with weaker survey coverage in that wave, so the modelled estimates should be read alongside posterior interval widths and original sample sizes. **Unit-level modelling** seeks to overcome this shortcoming by modelling the individual outcome directly using unit-level predictors present in the survey respondent data.

## Comparative analysis

To better understand how the FH results are produced, we can inspect the contribution of each of the model components. The diagnostics below examine how estimates change as predictors, spatial structure, and temporal structure are added, and then review uncertainty and hyperparameters to understand where the model is borrowing strength most strongly.

```{r}
#| label: fh-collate

model_output_frame <- model_data |>
  select(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    msoa_name,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    n
  )

fh_results <- imap_dfr(
  fh_fits,
  \(fit, model_name) {
    bind_cols(
      model_output_frame,
      as_tibble(fit$summary.fitted.values)
    ) |>
      transmute(
        model = model_name,
        area_id,
        time_id,
        msoa_name,
        direct_estimate,
        variance,
        n,
        fh_estimate = mean,
        fh_variance = sd^2,
        fh_lower = .data[["0.025quant"]],
        fh_upper = .data[["0.975quant"]],
        fh_ci_width = fh_upper - fh_lower
      )
  }
) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = names(model_formulas)))
```

### How Fay--Herriot model smoothes direct estimates

We start by comparing the direct estimates with M1, the temporal-spatial Fay-Herriot model with no area predictors, to understand how the FH model handles noisy direct estimates before adding predictors.

```{r}
#| label: fh-baseline-data

fh_wide <- fh_results |>
  # One row per area-time cell, with model outputs in separate columns.
  select(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    model,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    fh_estimate,
    fh_variance
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = model,
    values_from = c(fh_estimate, fh_variance),
    names_sep = "__"
  )

direct_to_m1 <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    direct_variance = variance,
    variance_change = .data[["fh_variance__M1 +TempSpatial"]] - variance
  )

wave_years <- sort(unique(fh_wide$time_id))
```

```{r}
#| label: fh-baseline-plot
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 12
#| out-width: "100%"

variance_change_limit <- max(abs(direct_to_m1$variance_change), na.rm = TRUE) * .5
direct_variance_limit <- max(direct_to_m1$direct_variance, na.rm = TRUE)

direct_to_m1_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(direct_to_m1, by = "area_id")

plot_m1_variance_change <- function(wave) {
  direct_to_m1_map_data |>
    filter(time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = variance_change), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = diverging_low,
      mid = "white",
      high = diverging_high,
      midpoint = 0,
      limits = c(-variance_change_limit, variance_change_limit),
      oob = squish,
      labels = variance_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Change"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

plot_direct_variance <- function(wave) {
  direct_to_m1_map_data |>
    filter(time_id == wave) |>
    ggplot() +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = direct_variance), colour = "transparent") +
    scale_fill_distiller(
      palette = "Reds",
      direction = 1,
      limits = c(0, direct_variance_limit),
      labels = variance_label,
      na.value = missing_fill,
      name = "Variance"
    ) +
    ggtitle(wave) +
    theme_void() +
    map_text_theme
}

variance_change_maps <- lapply(wave_years, plot_m1_variance_change)
direct_variance_maps <- lapply(wave_years, plot_direct_variance)

variance_change_maps[[1]] <- variance_change_maps[[1]] +
  ylab("Variance change")
direct_variance_maps[[1]] <- direct_variance_maps[[1]] +
  ylab("Direct variance")

for (i in seq_len(length(wave_years) - 1)) {
  variance_change_maps[[i]] <- variance_change_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
  direct_variance_maps[[i]] <- direct_variance_maps[[i]] +
    theme(legend.position = "none")
}

direct_to_m1_ranked <- direct_to_m1 |>
  drop_na(variance_change) |>
  group_by(time_id) |>
  arrange(direct_variance, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(variance_rank = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    time_id,
    variance_rank,
    `Variance change` = variance_change,
    `Variance (direct)` = direct_variance
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(time_id, variance_rank),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  )

direct_to_m1_ranked_plot <- ggplot(
  direct_to_m1_ranked,
  aes(
    x = variance_rank,
    y = value,
    colour = measure
  )
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(vars(time_id), nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = variance_label) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Variance change" = "purple",
    "Variance (direct)" = "red"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "",
    x = "MSOAs sorted by variance",
    y = "Variance",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  chart_text_theme

(wrap_plots(c(variance_change_maps, direct_variance_maps), ncol = 3) /
  direct_to_m1_ranked_plot) +
  plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1)) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Direct estimates compared with FH model (M1)",
    subtitle = "M1 stabilises noisy direct estimates with temporal-spatial smoothing",
    theme = map_annotation_theme
  )
```
Area-time cells with high sampling variance contain less reliable local information, so M1 pulls them more strongly toward the temporal-spatial model prediction. The Bayesian FH fit also produces posterior estimates for cells with missing direct estimates or zero/missing variance, allowing sparse or unsampled area-time cells to remain in the output with explicit uncertainty.

```{r}
#| label: fh-missing-direct
fh_wide |>
  filter(is.na(direct_estimate) | is.na(variance)) |>
  transmute(
    `MSOA` = area_id,
    `Wave year` = time_id,
    `Direct estimate` = share_label(direct_estimate),
    `Sampling variance` = round(variance, 6),
    `M1 estimate` = share_label(.data[["fh_estimate__M1 +TempSpatial"]]),
    `M1 posterior variance` = round(
      .data[["fh_variance__M1 +TempSpatial"]],
      6
    )
  )
```

### Adding Temporal And Spatial Effects

The contribution of the selected model's random effects can be examined through diagnostic outputs by `INLA`:

- `tau` is the precision of the random effect, or the inverse of its variance. Higher temporal `tau` than spatial means the temporal random effect varies less than spatial.
- `phi` is the BYM2 mixing parameter: it indicates how much of the area random effect is assigned to the structured spatial component versus the unstructured component. A low value here (less than `0.5`) means the unstructured components contribute much more to the area random effect.

```{r}
#| label: fh-hyper

fh_fits[[fh_best_model]]$summary.hyperpar |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "parameter") |>
  filter(str_detect(parameter, "time_inla_id|area_inla_id|Phi")) |>
  select(parameter, mean, sd, `0.025quant`, `0.5quant`, `0.975quant`) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

### Adding Predictors

Besides consulting WAIC, we can also inspect local estimate changes to see where the model moves the target estimates and whether those movements are substantively plausible. In Fay-Herriot SAE, adding predictors changes the expected value for each area-time cell, and unstable direct estimates are pulled more strongly toward those updated model predictions when the predictors are relevant.

Here we compare M1 with M3, which adds average age, population density, and car access.

```{r}
#| label: fh-predictor-change

predictor_change <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    estimate_change =
      .data[["fh_estimate__M3 +PopDensCarAccess"]] -
      .data[["fh_estimate__M1 +TempSpatial"]]
  ) |>
  distinct(area_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
```
```{r}
#| label: fh-map-change
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "100%"

predictor_change_estimate_limit <- quantile(
  abs(predictor_change$estimate_change),
  0.95,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  names = FALSE
)

msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(predictor_change, by = "area_id") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = estimate_change), colour = "transparent") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = diverging_low,
    mid = "white",
    high = diverging_high,
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-predictor_change_estimate_limit, predictor_change_estimate_limit),
    oob = squish,
    labels = pp_label,
    na.value = missing_fill,
    name = "Change"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Estimate change after adding additional predictors",
    subtitle = "M3 +PopDensCarAccess minus M1 +TempSpatial"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  map_text_theme
```
```{r}
#| label: fh-change-summary
model_data |>
  select(
    area_id,
    `Mean adult age` = scaled_mean_age_adult,
    `Population density` = scaled_population_density,
    `Car-access household share` = scaled_car_access_hhshare
  ) |>
  distinct(area_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  left_join(predictor_change, by = "area_id") |>
  mutate(
    change_group = case_when(
      estimate_change >= quantile(estimate_change, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) ~
        "Raised most with M3",
      estimate_change <= quantile(estimate_change, 0.1, na.rm = TRUE) ~
        "Lowered most with M3",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  drop_na(change_group) |>
  group_by(change_group) |>
  summarise(
    across(
      c(`Mean adult age`, `Population density`, `Car-access household share`),
      \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

The trend shown here is that the older, the less dense and the higher share of householdw owning a car an MSOA is, the lower the rate of frequently cycling. 

The coefficient table below reports the fixed-effect terms from the selected FH model, representing the expected percentage-point change in frequent cycling associated with a one-standard-deviation increase in that predictor.

```{r}
#| label: fh-fixed

fh_fits[[fh_best_model]]$summary.fixed |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "term") |>
  mutate(
    term = recode(
      term,
      `(Intercept)` = "Intercept",
      scaled_mean_age_adult = "Mean adult age",
      scaled_car_access_hhshare = "Car-access household share",
      scaled_population_density = "Population density"
    )
  ) |>
  transmute(
    term,
    mean = pp_label(mean),
    lower = pp_label(.data[["0.025quant"]]),
    upper = pp_label(.data[["0.975quant"]])
  )
```

In practice, the decision to pick the right SAE model specification should be assessed holistically using global model diagnostics, stepwise changes across models, and domain knowledge regarding the modelled outcome.

```{r}
#| label: fh-export
#| code-fold: true
write_csv(final_fh_results, file.path(base_path, "freqbike_estimates_fh.csv"))
```
